candidate: Bean common mosaic virus (peanut stripe strain; Potyvirus phaseovulgaris)
validation_notes: MEGAHIT contig SRR29854842_k141_4 (10216 nt): BLASTn 99.29% id to OR734859.1 over 9985 nt; all-read remap 154,038 fragments (MAPQ≥20 129,004).
competing_explanations: Real infection of the sampled plant (seed-/aphid-transmitted peanut pathogen); cross-sample bleed-through from another infected library on the same lane; reagent/lab contamination with viral RNA
limitations: Strong 3′ coverage bias (poly(A)/oligo-dT); Stage A MAPQ≈0 because BCMV isolates compete; Kraken2 splits reads across related potyvirus species names
source_evidence: 0.69% of all reads, 4,337x mean depth, 99.95% breadth at 1x; a 10.2 kb contig matches a peanut BCMV isolate at 99.3% nt. A known seed- and aphid-borne peanut pathogen in a peanut field sample. Bleed-through would need a neighbouring library with an even higher viral load to leak 0.69%; reagent RNA would not be a peanut-specific strain at near-complete coverage.

validation_notes: MEGAHIT contig SRR29854842_k141_5 (5851 nt): BLASTn 92.36% id to NC_034247.1 over 5718 nt; all-read remap 4,254 fragments (MAPQ≥20 4,233). aa id vs CPPV2: P0 83.5%, P1-P2 fusion 96.3%, P1 89.9%, protein 3a 93.5%, read-through 92.7%, coat 98.5%, movement 91.5%.
competing_explanations: Real infection (aphid-transmitted, phloem-limited); bleed-through; a divergent CPPV2 isolate vs. a distinct polerovirus species
limitations: Only one complete CPPV2 genome for comparison; identity 92–93% to closest reference; per-protein aa identity from tblastn, not curated ORFs
source_evidence: 180x depth, 95.8% breadth, a 5.85 kb near-complete contig; only ~92% nt identity to the CPPV2 RefSeq, with every ORF divergent (83-98% aa). A divergent field isolate argues against reagent or lab-strain contamination, and bleed-through would need another library carrying this same uncharacterized virus. Poleroviruses are aphid-transmitted plant pathogens. Possibly a new isolate or species, which makes it worth reporting.

gene_support: high: 8391 genes (≥5 frags: 5833), rRNA 7.28%; low: 3501 genes (≥5 frags: 1310), rRNA 5.42%
competing_explanations: Real associate (root/nodule pathogen or endophyte; nodules are soil-exposed); surface soil contamination of tissue; cross-sample bleed-through
limitations: Species/forma specialis unresolved (three F. oxysporum SC references within ~1% read share); genome breadth not informative for RNA-seq (gene-level counts used instead)
source_evidence: 2.29% of analyzed reads (48% of non-host), 99.1% mean identity, transcripts from 8,391 genes, so the fungus was alive and actively expressing genes. F. oxysporum is a common soil-borne root pathogen of peanut. Bleed-through is not credible at 2.3%, and dead reagent DNA would not yield poly(A) mRNA from thousands of genes. Internal infection versus surface soil is unresolved. Consequential because 2.3% of reads would distort normalization, assembly and DE if it varies across samples.

candidate: Bradyrhizobium (nodule rhizobia; high-identity subset closest to B. guangxiense)
gene_support: [vs Bgx_CCBAU53363] high: 338 genes (≥5 frags: 47), rRNA 86.65%; low: 337 genes (≥5 frags: 58), rRNA 96.20%
competing_explanations: Real nodule symbiont (expected in root nodules); conserved-rRNA cross-mapping from other Alphaproteobacteria
limitations: 77% of group fragments are <98% identity and 96% rRNA; high-identity subset still 87% rRNA; bacterial mRNA likely depleted by poly(A)-based library preparation
source_evidence: Expected nitrogen-fixing symbiont of peanut root nodules, with a high-identity subset closest to B. guangxiense, a peanut-nodulating species. Bradyrhizobium is also a kitome genus, but in nodule tissue the symbiont explanation is far more parsimonious. The low signal (0.18%, 87-96% rRNA) fits poly(A) selection depleting bacterial mRNA. Real but harmless to host analyses.

validation_notes: BCMV reads with mate on host 18S/28S rRNA: 25 pairs; end-to-end junction-spanning reads per contig: 0=2, 1=4, 2=1, 3=0.
competing_explanations: Library chimeras (ligation/PCR); assembler joins across rare chimeric reads; genuine virus–host recombinant RNA (implausible but listed)
limitations: Junction support counted only for end-to-end reads with ≤2 mismatches
source_evidence: The contigs join BCMV to host 18S/28S rRNA, yet only 0-4 end-to-end reads span each junction, and only 25 read pairs have a BCMV read with its mate on host rRNA. Against 129k BCMV fragments, such rare joins fit ligation/PCR chimeras that the assembler extended. A genuine virus-host recombinant would need consistent, abundant junction reads.

validation_notes: Human-confident pairs (MAPQ≥20, id≥0.98): 10,410; on chrM: 317; distinct nuclear sequences: 30. pct columns use human-confident pairs.
competing_explanations: Handling/operator contamination during sampling or library prep; reagent-borne human nucleic acid; bleed-through from a human library on the same lane; misassigned conserved eukaryotic reads (tested: identity ≥0.98 required)
limitations: Non-host pool only (human reads that also align to peanut are not counted); many confident pairs on rDNA-bearing contigs (chr21, chr22_KI270733v1_random)
source_evidence: 10,410 human-confident pairs (MAPQ>=20, identity >=0.98), including 317 on chrM, so the reads are truly human and not misassigned conserved eukaryotic sequence. The fraction (0.05%) is typical of operator handling. The same level as Cutibacterium (0.0485%), a skin commensal, points to a shared handling source. Too low to affect analyses.

competing_explanations: Human skin commensal introduced during handling; reagent/kit contaminant (well-known 'kitome' member); real plant-associated propionibacteria (less likely at ≥99% identity to C. acnes)
limitations: Group also attracts C. granulosum and lower-identity relatives; counts are label-level
source_evidence: 97.9% identity to C. acnes, the dominant human skin commensal, at exactly the same fraction as the human reads (0.0485%), which points to one handling event. A reagent (kitome) origin remains possible. A plant-associated propionibacterium is unlikely at this identity to C. acnes. Low level and harmless.

competing_explanations: Real rhizosphere/endophytic actinobacteria on or in nodules; soil carried on tissue; reagent contaminant
limitations: Only one Streptomyces reference in panel (genus is huge); species unresolved; mean identity 0.957
source_evidence: Detected by all 3 screens, but at only 95.7% identity to the single panel reference. That fits an environmental strain from a large genus, not a lab or reagent strain. Streptomyces are typical rhizosphere/endophytic actinobacteria, and nodules come straight out of soil. 0.14% of reads; harmless.

competing_explanations: Real soil/rhizosphere fungus on nodule surface; airborne lab contaminant (common Eurotiales mould); cross-mapping from the abundant Fusarium (competitor included)
limitations: Species unresolved (three references; mean identity 0.961); cellular RNA breadth not informative
source_evidence: Detected by all 3 screens at 96.1-96.9% identity, with the abundant Fusarium included as a competitor, which rules out cross-mapping. A common soil/rhizosphere fungus on soil-exposed nodules. An airborne lab mould is possible but less parsimonious given the field origin. 0.15% of reads; harmless.

competing_explanations: Laboratory/reagent E. coli DNA/RNA (e.g. enzyme production strains); real enteric bacteria on field tissue; database error (Kraken2 'Salmonella' vs better E. coli mapping)
limitations: Low counts; E. coli Sakai is one representative of a diverse species
source_evidence: Reads map better to E. coli than to Salmonella, so the Kraken2 'Salmonella' label is a classifier artifact. E. coli nucleic acid is a standard carry-over from recombinant enzyme production. Low counts (0.007%) and patchy breadth fit reagent carry-over better than a colonizing enteric. Harmless.

competing_explanations: Database/classifier error on AT-rich or low-complexity reads; genuine apicomplexan (implausible for peanut nodules)
limitations: Near-identical fragments define support; local alignments soft-clip low-identity ends
source_evidence: Only 2 near-identical fragments of 5,240; the rest are soft-clipped local alignments. Only Kraken2 supports it (77 pairs). An apicomplexan blood parasite has no plausible route into peanut nodules, so these are AT-rich or low-complexity reads misclassified.

candidate: Bacteria-classified k-mer reads (STAT: 267,551 Bacteria clade, 255,756 domain-only)
validation_notes: Kraken2 (all 8,497,015 trimmed pairs): Bacteria clade 198,207 pairs, of which 197,247 (99.52%) align to the peanut assembly and 960 are unmapped; domain-only 61,820 pairs, 99.88% host-aligned. Organelle-only mapping: 887,167 pairs (10.4409%) organelle-like.
competing_explanations: Host DNA with bacterial-like k-mers (organellar DNA and nuclear plastid/mitochondrial insertions; conserved genes); real bacterial DNA
limitations: Per-read test uses Kraken2 (no plant genomes) as a stand-in for STAT; host classes from step 11
source_evidence: 99.52% of the Bacteria-clade pairs and 99.88% of the domain-only pairs align to the peanut assembly, and 10.4% of all pairs are organelle-like. The 'bacterial' k-mers are host organellar DNA (endosymbiotic in origin) and nuclear plastid/mitochondrial insertions (NUPTs/NUMTs). They were flagged only because Kraken2 and STAT lack plant genomes. Real bacterial DNA is at most 960 unmapped pairs.

validation_notes: Human-confident pairs (MAPQ≥20, id≥0.98): 6; on chrM: 0; distinct nuclear sequences: 4. pct columns use human-confident pairs.
competing_explanations: Handling contamination; Kraken2 misassignment of non-human reads
source_evidence: Kraken2 assigns 1,712 pairs to human, but only 6 meet the human-confident threshold (0 on chrM, 4 distinct sequences), and STAT finds none. The Kraken2 call is misassignment of non-human reads, and the 6 reads are below any credible level.

competing_explanations: Real phyllosphere bacterium on leaves (Sphingomonas is a common leaf colonist); reagent contaminant (Sphingomonas is also a common kitome genus)
source_evidence: 15 near-identical fragments at 97.1% identity, supported by 2 screens. Sphingomonas is among the commonest leaf (phyllosphere) colonists and fits field leaf tissue. It is also a kitome genus, so reagent origin is the main alternative; there is no extraction blank to separate them. Very low (0.0003%); harmless.
